title: Narada and the far shore
hookLine: a sage who has read everything is still in sorrow, and the last step across is what he takes in
carry: everything you take in feeds the mind
last: THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.

cards: The sage Narada comes to the teacher Sanatkumara with a long list. The four Vedas, the old stories, grammar, mathematics, the stars, the arts. I've learned all of it, he says, and I'm still in sorrow.
I know words, not the self, and I've heard that the one who knows the self crosses over sorrow. Take me across. The seventh chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad is the long road across.
And at the very end, the last step it gives Narada isn't another book. It's what he takes in.

teach.b: Here's the chain, paraphrased. When what is taken in is pure, the inner being is pure. When the inner being is pure, memory becomes steady.
When memory is steady, all the knots are loosened. In Sanskrit it begins aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih.
Ahara is what's taken in. Sattva is the inner being, the mind at its clearest.
And the text adds: to Narada, his stains wiped away, Sanatkumara showed the far shore beyond darkness. Notice three things. First, the direction.
It runs from the plate inward, from something as plain as a meal to the very thing Narada came for: crossing over sorrow. Second, memory here isn't remembering where the keys are.
Readers in the Vedanta tradition take it as a steady remembering of who one really is: the self, atman, the thing Narada admitted he didn't know. Third, the knots. The text doesn't name them.
Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears. Then the scholar's turn.
Shankara, the great Vedanta teacher, reads ahara more widely than food: everything gathered in by the senses, what the eyes take in, what the ears take in. Pure intake, not just a pure plate.

This is ahara shuddhi, purity of what's taken in. It's why many Hindus take care over what they eat and offer it first, and why many teachers apply the same care to what a person watches and listens to.
Narada had filled himself with words and stayed in sorrow. The chain says: watch what you take in, and the way across gets clearer.

how: Some Hindus cite the Chandogya's line aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih to explain care about what and how they eat, and Vedanta teachers following Shankara apply it to everything a person takes in through the senses.

o: a strict fast that loosens every knot all by itself
eating only pure foods, while the rest stays the same
taking in with care: pure intake, a clear mind, knots loosened

games.q: the chain, link by link — tap the pairs.
p: everything taken in by the senses

s: the Chandogya's chain starts from food and ends at the loosening of knots
pure food, pure inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened.
the memory in this line means remembering where the keys are
it's a steady remembering of what matters, of who one really is.
Shankara reads ahara as food alone
he reads it as everything gathered in: what the eyes, ears and mind take in.

games.q: you're Narada. you've studied everything there is, and you're still in sorrow. what do you do?
o: go to a teacher and admit it.
games.why: he goes to Sanatkumara and admits he knows only words. the chapter ends with the chain from pure food to loosened knots, and the far shore beyond darkness.

practice: Go back through the day so far, not only meals: what the eyes took in, a screen, a street, a face, and what the ears took in, voices, music, news, letting each pass without grading it.
Then find one knot somewhere, a tightness something left behind, and with each breath out let it loosen a little, if it will. If you pray, hold that knot in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. In the Chandogya's chain, pure intake, a clear inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2: when what is taken in is pure, the inner being is pure.

carryVoice: Your line: everything you take in feeds the mind. Ahara, not just the plate. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.2–3 (Narada lists what he has studied, knows only words, not the self; the knower of the self crosses sorrow; he asks Sanatkumara to take him across)
Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2 (aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih: pure food, pure inner being, steady memory, release of all knots; the far shore beyond darkness)
Shankara's commentary on Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2 (ahara as what is gathered in, the perception of sense objects)
